title: Why Your Critical Path Changes When Production Changes
description:
A planned completion date looks reasonable until one operation runs late, a material release slips or a resource disappears, and every downstream promise moves with it. This episode shows manufacturing planners and IT/OT architects how to apply critical path thinking to live production, from shared machines and quality holds to MES, ERP, Microsoft Fabric and knowledge graphs, so they can see which dependency controls delivery now.
In this episode
00:00 – Introduction: when the plan meets production05:20 – One late operation and the delivery date11:16 – What critical path means on the shop floor22:43 – Material, shared machines, people and readiness51:41 – Quality holds and engineering changes68:15 – Why dashboards don't solve dependency problems85:27 – Data model, digital twin and knowledge graph96:07 – Prediction, scheduling, optimization and trade-offs
Key takeaways
In production the critical path is the chain of remaining dependencies that controls the earliest completion date right now, and it moves when machines, material, people or quality conditions change.A routing, a status dashboard or a Power BI report shows intent and symptoms, but a live dependency model with explicit links between orders, operations, resources and release conditions is needed to explain why a date moved.Prediction, scheduling and optimization answer different questions, and generative AI should explain schedule results rather than invent the schedule itself.
Worth quoting
“An operation can report late and still not threaten the due date if there's time later in the route.” – Mirko Peters (09:44)
“The route tells you where the part should go, it doesn't tell you when the part can actually go there.” – Mirko Peters (19:21)
